questions.question: What are the four topics listed in 'This chapter covers'?
questions.answer: The limitations of deep learning; the nature of intelligence; what's missing from current approaches; what the future might look like.
questions.explanation: Listed in the box on the page.

questions.question: Why does the author begin with limitations before discussing the future?
questions.answer: Because using a tool appropriately requires knowing what it can't do, and the gaps define what future approaches must add.
questions.explanation: Paraphrases the introduction.

questions.question: How does the author characterize his thoughts on the future of AI?
options: As established consensus
As speculative
As experimental results
As product announcements
questions.answer: As speculative
questions.explanation: He says he will 'offer some speculative thoughts'.

questions.question: Before reading on, list three things you suspect deep learning models struggle with. Compare after reading section 19.1.
questions.answer: Open-ended.
questions.explanation: Section 19.1 names novelty, phrasing sensitivity, generalizable programs and anthropomorphizing.

questions.question: For which kind of reader does the author say this chapter should be especially interesting?
questions.answer: Readers who would like to get into fundamental research.
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of the intro paragraph.

questions.question: According to the page, why are deep learning models inherently poor at adaptation?
options: Because they have too few parameters
Because their parameters are frozen after training, making them a static database
Because they are trained with gradient descent, which is slow
Because they cannot process images
questions.answer: Because their parameters are frozen after training, making them a static database
questions.explanation: The page ties the weakness to the static, backward-looking database. Parameter count, training speed and modality are not the stated reasons.

questions.question: What does the leopard-print sofa example illustrate?
questions.answer: That a model breaks down on inputs outside its training distribution: an ImageNet model labels the sofa a leopard because sofas (with such a texture) were not in its training data.
questions.explanation: Given as the example of a model failing out of distribution.

questions.question: What does the author mean by saying an LLM's ability 'has nothing to do with problem complexity, and everything to do with familiarity'?
questions.answer: Whether an LLM solves a problem depends on how closely it resembles patterns in its training data, not on how hard it is; simple novel problems can defeat it.
questions.explanation: Illustrated by the figure 19.1 puzzle.

questions.question: Why did ChatGPT answer that 10 kilos of steel and one kilo of feathers weigh the same?
questions.answer: The classic trick question ('one kilo of steel or one kilo of feathers?') with the answer 'the same' appears many times online; the model retrieved that memorized answer instead of reading the changed quantity.
questions.explanation: The page explains it as a failure on a tiny variation of a frequently seen pattern.

questions.question: How does the author explain what LLMs do during 'in-context learning'?
options: They update their weights from the prompt
They fetch vector functions memorized during training and reapply them
They run a symbolic search over programs
They query an external database
questions.answer: They fetch vector functions memorized during training and reapply them
questions.explanation: Stated on the page. LLMs do not update weights in context; symbolic search and external databases are not mentioned here.

questions.question: Can you think of a task from your own work that a model handled well only because it was familiar, and a simple variant it might fail on?
questions.answer: Open-ended.
questions.explanation: Apply the familiarity-vs-complexity lens from this page.

questions.question: In Figure 19.2, the host opens door No. 1, the door the contestant picked, and reveals a car. What is the correct answer to 'Is it to your advantage to change your choice?'
options: Yes, switching wins with probability 2/3
It makes no difference; both choices win with probability 1/2
No, you already have the car, so switching loses with certainty
Yes, switching wins with probability 1/3
questions.answer: No, you already have the car, so switching loses with certainty
questions.explanation: The car is behind the chosen door, so the other two doors hide goats: staying wins with probability 1. The 2/3 answer is the canonical Monty Hall answer, which is what the model in the figure gave; it applies only when the host reveals a goat behind a door you did not pick. 1/2 is the common wrong intuition for the original puzzle. 1/3 is the probability of the initial pick in the original puzzle, not a switching probability here.

questions.question: Why did early ChatGPT say that 10 kilos of steel and one kilo of feathers weigh the same?
questions.answer: Because the classic trick question ('one kilo of steel or one kilo of feathers?', answer: same weight) appears many times online. The model recognized the familiar form and repeated the memorized answer without attending to the changed number.
questions.explanation: The book says the model 'would just repeat the answer it had memorized without paying any attention to the actual numbers in the query, or what the query really meant' (p.589-590).

questions.question: The book claims an LLM's ability to solve a problem has 'nothing to do with problem complexity, and everything to do with familiarity.' How do Figure 19.1 and Figure 19.2 support this claim from two different directions?
questions.answer: Figure 19.1 is a simple but novel problem that models fail: low complexity does not help when the problem is unfamiliar. Figure 19.2 is a problem that looks very familiar but has a changed detail; the model gives the familiar answer even though it is now wrong: familiarity of form dominates over the actual content.
questions.explanation: One example shows that easy-but-new fails; the other shows that a familiar surface triggers a memorized answer even when the logic has changed. Together they point to retrieval by similarity rather than reasoning.

questions.question: According to the page, how were the specific failing prompts (steel/feathers, Monty Hall variant) fixed?
options: By changing the Transformer architecture
By special-casing them, using human-written training data for failure cases
By increasing the model's context length
By adding a symbolic reasoning module
questions.answer: By special-casing them, using human-written training data for failure cases
questions.explanation: The book says the prompts 'were patched later on by special-casing them' and mentions over 25,000 people reviewing failures and suggesting better answers. No architectural change, context length change or symbolic module is mentioned; section 19.4 later discusses symbolic approaches as a future direction, not as the fix used here.

questions.question: Why does the book call LLM maintenance 'a constant game of whack-a-mole'?
questions.answer: Because each fix only covers a specific failing prompt; the general inability to handle variants remains, so new failures keep appearing, including small variations of prompts that were already patched (p.591).
questions.explanation: Patching adds memorized correct answers near the failing case, but does not give the model a general mechanism for adapting to new variants. The number of possible variants is unbounded.

questions.question: Write your own variant of a famous riddle or textbook puzzle in which one small change flips the correct answer. Predict what a retrieval-based model would answer and explain why.
questions.answer: Example: 'A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1.00. How much does the ball cost?' (here $0.10 is correct, unlike the famous version where the bat costs $1.00 *more* than the ball, giving $0.05). A retrieval-based model might answer $0.05.
questions.explanation: A good variant keeps the wording close to the famous version (so it lands near the memorized item in latent space) while changing the logic. This mirrors the steel/feathers and Monty Hall examples on this page.

questions.question: Which technique from chapter 10 does the book say is the basis for creating adversarial examples?
options: Class activation heatmaps
Gradient ascent in input space
Data augmentation
Fine-tuning the top layers of a pretrained model
questions.answer: Gradient ascent in input space
questions.explanation: The page reminds the reader that gradient ascent in input space was used to generate inputs maximizing a filter's activation (filter visualization) and that the same process aimed at a class prediction yields adversarial examples. Heatmaps visualize where a class is detected but don't create new inputs. Data augmentation and fine-tuning change the training process or the weights, not a test input.

questions.question: Describe the three images in Figure 19.3 and what the model predicts for each.
questions.answer: Left: the original panda photo, predicted 'Panda'. Middle: the gibbon class gradient (noise-like, with a gibbon photo below it indicating which class it targets). Right: the adversarial example (panda + gradient), which looks like the original panda but is predicted 'Gibbon!'.
questions.explanation: The figure shows that an imperceptible change in the image upends the classification, as the caption says.

questions.question: In training, filter visualization and adversarial example generation, what is held fixed and what is changed?
questions.answer: Training: input fixed, weights changed to reduce loss. Filter visualization: weights fixed, input changed (from noise) to increase a filter activation. Adversarial example: weights fixed, input changed (from a real image) to increase a wrong class's score, with a small perturbation.
questions.explanation: All three use gradients; the last two use gradients with respect to the input, which is why the book calls adversarial examples a direct consequence of the chapter-10 technique.

questions.question: What two conclusions does the book draw from the panda/gibbon example?
options: Models need more data and larger architectures
Models are brittle, and their input-to-output mapping differs deeply from human perception
Gibbons and pandas share visual features that humans miss
Adversarial examples only affect small models
questions.answer: Models are brittle, and their input-to-output mapping differs deeply from human perception
questions.explanation: The text says this 'evidences both the brittleness of these models and the deep difference between their input-to-output mapping and our human perception.' The book does not suggest that more data fixes this (p.595 argues scale does not). The perturbation is not a real shared feature. Nothing restricts the phenomenon to small models.

questions.question: A model's gibbon logit is approximately linear around an image, $s(x) = w^\top x$. You change every pixel by $\pm\epsilon$ following the sign of $w$. If the image has 10,000 pixel values, $\epsilon = 0.01$, and the average $|w_i|$ is 0.05, how much does the logit increase?
questions.answer: $\epsilon \sum_i |w_i| = 0.01 \times 0.05 \times 10{,}000 = 5$ logits.
questions.explanation: Moving each coordinate by $\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(w_i)$ adds $\epsilon |w_i|$ to the score per coordinate. The sum over many dimensions is large even though each change is tiny. This is an AI-added illustration of why the imperceptible change in Figure 19.3 can flip the class.

questions.question: Can you explain, without notes, how the LLM sensitivity introduced at the bottom of this page is analogous to adversarial images?
questions.answer: In both cases a change that is irrelevant to a human (invisible pixel noise; different names or wording) moves the input to a different region of the model's input space, where the model behaves differently. The model does not respond to meaning as a human would.
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says 'Similarly, LLMs suffer from an extremely high sensitivity to minor details in their prompts,' and p.592 develops this with the Alice riddle and prompt engineering.

questions.question: Alice has 7 brothers and 4 sisters. How many sisters does one of Alice's brothers have, and which number in the question is irrelevant?
questions.answer: 5 sisters (M + 1 = 4 + 1). The number of brothers, N = 7, is irrelevant.
questions.explanation: From the brother's view, his sisters are Alice's 4 sisters plus Alice. The page gives the answer as M + 1.

questions.question: According to the book, why do LLMs answer the Alice riddle correctly for N = 3 and M = 2 but often fail for other values?
options: Larger numbers exceed the model's arithmetic precision
Values like N = 3, M = 2 are common in online instances of the riddle, so the model has seen them
The riddle is ambiguous for other values
The tokenizer cannot encode other digits
questions.answer: Values like N = 3, M = 2 are common in online instances of the riddle, so the model has seen them
questions.explanation: The page says values 'commonly found in online instances of the riddle' generally give correct answers. The arithmetic is trivial (one addition), so precision is not the issue. The riddle is equally clear for any values. Tokenizers can encode all digits.

questions.question: In the 'Answer like a pirate' example, what two things does the prompt retrieve from the LLM's database?
questions.answer: A piece of knowledge (how to sort a list in Python) and a style transfer program ('Answer like a pirate'), which is then executed on the knowledge.
questions.explanation: The book describes the prompt as a database lookup that first retrieves knowledge and then retrieves and executes a style-transfer program.

questions.question: Explain the book's argument that the need for prompt engineering shows LLMs don't understand requests.
questions.answer: The information about the target task is the same across rewordings ('rewrite' vs. 'rephrase', with or without 'Think step by step'). An agent that understood the task would perform equally well on all of them. LLMs don't: performance depends on which address the wording points to, so you must search over wordings. Needing that search shows the model fetches programs by address rather than understanding intent.
questions.explanation: This combines the last paragraph of p.592 with its completion on p.593.

questions.question: Which comparison does the book use for prompt engineering?
options: Tuning hyperparameters with grid search
Trying different keywords when doing a Google search
Writing unit tests for a program
Translating between two programming languages
questions.answer: Trying different keywords when doing a Google search
questions.explanation: The page says prompt engineering 'is no different from trying different keywords when doing a Google search.' The other options are plausible analogies but are not what the book uses; grid search is the closest in spirit (trial-and-error search) but is not mentioned.

questions.question: Why does the interpolative nature of the LLM's stored programs make the first prompt unlikely to be optimal?
questions.answer: Because there is a continuum of nearby locations, each holding a slightly different version of the program, and thousands of possible wordings land at different ones. Nothing makes the location of your first wording the best one for your task.
questions.explanation: The book: 'There is no a priori reason for your first, naive prompt to be optimal for your task... it's merely going to fetch the program that your prompt points to, among many possible locations you could have landed on.'

questions.question: Think of a prompt you have reworded to get a better LLM answer. Can you describe that experience in the book's terms (address, latent space, search)?
questions.answer: Each rewording was a new address in latent space; the better answer came from a location holding a better-suited program; the process of rewording was a manual search.
questions.explanation: Mapping your own experience onto the book's model checks that you can apply it, not just repeat it.

questions.question: What does the book identify as the reason a Transformer trained on many digit-addition examples still makes mistakes?
options: Insufficient training epochs
It interpolates between training points instead of encoding the exact addition algorithm
The tokenizer splits numbers incorrectly
The learning rate is too high to converge
questions.answer: It interpolates between training points instead of encoding the exact addition algorithm
questions.explanation: The page says the Transformer 'doesn't manage to encode the exact addition algorithm... It is instead guessing the output by interpolating between the data points it has seen.' The other options are training or preprocessing issues that the book does not invoke; the book's point is that more of the same training wouldn't change the nature of what is learned.

questions.question: What observation about LLM addition accuracy suggests memorization rather than an algorithm?
questions.answer: Accuracy depends strongly on which digits are added, with more common digits giving higher accuracy. A true algorithm would be equally accurate for all digits.
questions.explanation: Dependence on frequency in the training data is the signature of memorization/interpolation.

questions.question: Why is a 'static chain of simple, continuous geometric transformations' a poor fit for addition with carrying?
questions.answer: Carrying is discrete (a carry happens or not) and sequential (a carry can propagate across many columns, requiring a number of steps that grows with the number length). A continuous map approximates sharp, discrete changes poorly, and a static network performs a fixed amount of computation regardless of how many sequential steps are needed.
questions.explanation: The book says this kind of model fits perceptual pattern recognition but is 'a very poor fit for encoding any sort of step-by-step discrete logic, such as concepts like place value or carrying over.'

questions.question: The book says most programs can't be expressed as deep learning models. Which pair of reasons does it give?
options: Networks are too slow and too large to deploy
No network of reasonable size solves the task, or one exists but isn't learnable (too complex a transform or no appropriate data)
Programs use integers while networks use floats
Programs need memory and networks have none
questions.answer: No network of reasonable size solves the task, or one exists but isn't learnable (too complex a transform or no appropriate data)
questions.explanation: This is stated at the end of 19.1.3. Speed and deployment are not mentioned. Number types and memory are plausible technical distinctions but not the reasons the book gives.

questions.question: How does limitation 3 (programs that don't generalize) differ from limitations 1 and 2 (novelty and phrasing)?
questions.answer: Limitations 1 and 2 concern reaching the right program: there may be none for a novel problem, or small changes in phrasing may land you at a different one. Limitation 3 holds even when you know exactly how to address a well-known program: the program itself is unreliable, working for some input values and failing for others.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph of 19.1.3 makes exactly this contrast ('Even if you just need to query and apply a well-known program, and you know exactly how to address this program in latent space...').

questions.question: Compute 4357 + 8936 by the school algorithm and count how many columns produce a carry.
questions.answer: 13293; three columns produce a carry (ones: 13, hundreds: 12, thousands: 13). The tens column (5+3+1 = 9) does not.
questions.explanation: This is the example from the page, worked out to show the discrete carry decisions that the book says continuous models struggle to encode.

questions.question: Can you explain in your own words what 'your prompt is but an address in an infinite ocean of programs' means and why the programs are 'a by-product'?
questions.answer: The model stores a continuum of programs; a prompt selects one location. The programs were not designed or taught explicitly; they emerged because they helped the model predict the next token across a huge corpus.
questions.explanation: Linking the prompt-as-address view (p.592) to how the programs were acquired explains why there's no guarantee the selected program does what you intended.

questions.question: In Figure 19.4, against which stage does the model get a check mark?
options: Real world
Embodied human experience
Abstract concepts in human mind
Labeled data exemplifying these concepts
questions.answer: Labeled data exemplifying these concepts
questions.explanation: The model 'matches the training data' (check mark). Against the human concepts it gets a not-equal sign ('doesn't match the human mental model it came from'), and against the real world a question mark ('may not always transfer well'). Embodied experience has no evaluation arrow.

questions.question: What is 'theory of mind', and what example does the book give?
questions.answer: Our tendency to project intentions, beliefs and knowledge onto things around us. Example: drawing a smiley face on a rock makes it 'happy' in our minds.
questions.explanation: The book applies this to language models: we're led to believe they understand their word sequences the way we do.

questions.question: The book says networks were trained on 'a different, far narrower task than the one we wanted to teach them.' What are the two tasks?
questions.answer: The task we want is the general concept or skill (e.g. recognizing an object, answering questions correctly). The task they are trained on is mapping training inputs to training targets, point by point.
questions.explanation: Training only optimizes the second, so behavior outside the training data is not guaranteed, which is why deviations can break the model in absurd ways.

questions.question: What does the book mean by 'The models you create will take any shortcut available to fit their training data'?
options: Models train faster than expected
Models will use any feature that fits the labels, even if it isn't what defines the concept
Models skip some training examples
Models prefer smaller architectures
questions.answer: Models will use any feature that fits the labels, even if it isn't what defines the concept
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the point that the learned mapping is a simplistic sketch of human concepts. Training speed, skipping examples and architecture size are unrelated to the claim.

questions.question: Why does each step in Figure 19.4 make the model a 'dim' image of the original concept?
questions.answer: Each step loses information: human concepts summarize experience of the real world; labeled data captures only finite examples of those concepts; the model sees only the data, so it can only reconstruct what the examples constrain, and fills the rest with whatever fits (shortcuts).
questions.explanation: This is the reasoning behind the figure's 'matches the training data' but 'doesn't match the human mental model' annotations.

questions.question: What question opens section 19.2, and when did the opposing narrative peak according to the book?
questions.answer: 'Could we just keep scaling our models to overcome the limitations of deep learning? Is scale all we need?' The 'scale is all you need' narrative was especially prominent in early 2023, at peak LLM hype, when GPT-4 had just been released.
questions.explanation: The section title, 'Scale isn't all you need', gives away the book's answer, developed on p.595.

questions.question: Recall a time when you were surprised by an AI system's failure. Can you explain the surprise using the book's theory-of-mind argument?
questions.answer: The surprise came from assuming the system understood the task as a person would (because its outputs looked human), while it had only learned to map training-like inputs to outputs. The failing input deviated from the training patterns.
questions.explanation: The book: 'Then we're surprised when any slight departure from the patterns present in the training data causes the model to generate completely absurd answers.'

questions.question: What is the book's main objection to using scaling laws as evidence that scale leads to general intelligence?
options: Scaling laws are statistically invalid
The benchmarks used to measure performance are effectively memorization tests
Larger models are too expensive to train
Scaling laws only apply to vision models
questions.answer: The benchmarks used to measure performance are effectively memorization tests
questions.explanation: The page says 'the benchmarks they're using to measure performance are effectively memorization tests.' The book does not call scaling laws invalid; cost is discussed in chapter 16 but is not the objection here; scaling laws are discussed for LLMs, not just vision.

questions.question: List the three fundamental problems that the book says scaling won't solve.
questions.answer: (1) Models are limited to interpolative programs memorized at training time and can't synthesize new programs at inference time for novel situations. (2) Even in known situations these programs generalize poorly, causing oversensitivity to phrasing and confounder features. (3) Models are limited in what they can represent: most programs, especially algorithmic reasoning, can't be expressed as a continuous geometric morphing of a data manifold.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets on the page; they restate 19.1.1, 19.1.2 and 19.1.3.

questions.question: Why does the book think four to five orders of magnitude of scaling made no progress on these problems?
questions.answer: Because the problems are inherent to curve fitting, and the models are still the same kind of thing: parametric curves fitted to a dataset by gradient descent, using the Transformer architecture. Scaling changes size and knowledge, not the paradigm.
questions.explanation: The page: 'We have not made any progress on these problems because the models we're using are still the same.'

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the issues the book says scaling has failed to address?
options: Inability to adapt to novelty
Oversensitivity to phrasing
Inability to infer generalizable programs for reasoning problems
Lack of factual knowledge
questions.answer: Lack of factual knowledge
questions.explanation: The book lists the first three; it says models are now 'more knowledgeable', so knowledge has improved with scale. The point is that knowledge is not the same as adaptability.

questions.question: Suppose a scaling law gives loss $L \propto N^{-0.08}$. By what factor does the loss change if the model becomes 10,000 times larger? Does this, by itself, say anything about the three fundamental problems?
questions.answer: $10{,}000^{-0.08} = 10^{-0.32} \approx 0.48$: the loss roughly halves. By itself it says nothing about the three problems, since the loss measures fit to data like the training distribution.
questions.explanation: Power laws give predictable, diminishing improvements. The book's argument is about what is being measured: better fit to familiar data (memorization) doesn't imply adaptation to novelty. The formula is an AI-added illustration; the book gives none.

questions.question: According to the start of 19.2.1, what is the difference between humans and deep learning models beyond the fact that humans learn from embodied experience?
questions.answer: The human brain is 'an entirely different beast compared to a differentiable parametric function': humans do not simply apply a fixed geometric morphing from input to output.
questions.explanation: The book says the difference 'isn't just' embodiment; it's the nature of the system itself, which the following pages develop (automatons vs. intelligent agents, local vs. extreme generalization).

questions.question: Could you design a benchmark result that would convince the author that scaling had made progress on bullet 1? What property must the benchmark have?
questions.answer: It must test substantially novel tasks that can't be solved by memorized programs (e.g. new tasks not in any training data, like ARC puzzles), and a scaled-up model would need to improve on it without test-time search or special-casing.
questions.explanation: The book's critique is that standard benchmarks are memorization tests; a convincing benchmark must resist memorization, which is the design goal of ARC (p.605).

questions.question: According to the page, what was the original function of brains when they appeared more than half a billion years ago?
questions.answer: To store and execute behavioral programs: sets of 'If this happens, then do that' instructions linking sensory inputs to motor controls.
questions.explanation: The text says brains 'originally appeared ... as a way to store and execute behavioral programs' and defines those programs as reactive if-then rules connecting senses to motor controls.

questions.question: In the author's analogy, what plays the role of the 'source code' of early brains' behavioral programs?
options: Neural connectivity patterns
DNA
Sensory input
Natural selection
questions.answer: DNA
questions.explanation: The page states that 'the original "source code" of these programs was DNA, which would get decoded as neural connectivity patterns.' Neural connectivity is the compiled or running form of the program, not its source. Sensory input is the program's input. Natural selection is the programmer (p.597: 'Evolution was the programmer'), not the code.

questions.question: Why does the author call the ability of evolution to 'search over behavior space in a largely unbounded way' a major evolutionary shift?
questions.answer: Because DNA encodes neural wiring, and wiring is a general computing substrate, small genetic changes can produce very different behavioral programs. The space of behaviors evolution can explore by trial and error and selection therefore becomes vastly larger than before.
questions.explanation: The page links DNA to connectivity patterns and connectivity to behavior. p.597 adds that neural connectivity is 'a very general computing substrate', so evolution can find programs for any sensors or limbs. That expressiveness is what makes the search 'unbounded'.

questions.question: Map each element of the brain-evolution story onto deep learning: the programmer, the program storage, and the search signal.
questions.answer: Programmer: natural selection, corresponding to gradient descent. Program storage: neural connectivity, corresponding to the network's weights. Search signal: survival and reproduction, corresponding to the training loss.
questions.explanation: The page and p.597 describe evolution programming brains by trial and error, and p.597 explicitly puts a trained deep network in the same category as these early brains. The mapping makes clear that both produce fixed programs from an external optimization process.

questions.question: What does Figure 19.5 depict, according to its caption?
options: A deep neural network trained to imitate a worm
The brain network of the C. elegans worm, a behavioral automaton 'programmed' by natural evolution
The human cortex during abstract reasoning
A random graph used as a baseline for network control theory
questions.answer: The brain network of the C. elegans worm, a behavioral automaton 'programmed' by natural evolution
questions.explanation: The caption says exactly this and credits Emma Towlson and Yan et al. (Nature, 2017). The other options are inventions: it is not an artificial network, not a human brain, and not a random baseline.

questions.question: In Figure 19.5's legend, which four kinds of nodes are distinguished, and which roughly correspond to 'input', 'hidden processing' and 'output'?
questions.answer: Sensory neurons (input), interneurons (hidden processing), motor neurons and muscles (output).
questions.explanation: The legend lists sensory neuron, interneuron, motor neuron and muscle. Mapping them to input, hidden and output layers is an interpretive aid, not a claim the book makes.

questions.question: Explain in your own words why a system can be the product of an extremely powerful optimization process and still be 'just' an automaton.
questions.answer: Open answer. A good answer separates the search (evolution or gradient descent) from its product (fixed wiring or weights). The product only encodes behaviors that the search found useful in the situations it encountered, so it cannot generate new behavior for situations outside that set.
questions.explanation: This is the conceptual bridge from this page to the automaton definition on p.597 and the local-generalization discussion on p.598.

questions.question: Which of these does the author NOT list as a way an automaton's program can be produced?
options: Human-written programs
Evolution-generated programs
Fitting a model on a training dataset
On-the-fly recombination of abstractions at test time
questions.answer: On-the-fly recombination of abstractions at test time
questions.explanation: The parenthesis in 19.2.2 lists human-written programs, evolution-generated programs, and 'the implicit programming process of fitting a model on a training dataset.' On-the-fly recombination is what the author associates with intelligence (p.602), the opposite of an automaton.

questions.question: Define extreme generalization in the author's words.
questions.answer: An ability to adapt to novel, never-before-experienced situations using little data or even no new data at all, made possible by abstraction and reasoning.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the paragraph beginning 'This ability to use abstraction and reasoning...'.

questions.question: Why does the author group a trained deep neural network with a thermostat and a list-sorting program?
questions.answer: All three execute a fixed program for a specific context and cannot adapt on the fly when facing something they weren't 'programmed' for. The deep net's program was written implicitly by training, but it is still static at use time.
questions.explanation: The page defines automatons as static and context-specific, and says they fail outside their programming 'whether we're talking about human-written programs, evolution-generated programs, or the implicit programming process of fitting a model'.

questions.question: According to the page, how do you tell a student who memorized past exams from one who understands the material?
options: Give them the past exams again under time pressure
Give them a brand-new problem
Ask them to explain their answers to old questions
Compare their scores over three years
questions.answer: Give them a brand-new problem
questions.explanation: The author answers his own question: 'You give them a brand-new problem.' Repeating old exams or comparing scores can't separate the two, because memorization produces the same results on familiar questions. Explanations of old answers could also be memorized.

questions.question: List the specific human capabilities the author says go beyond 'mapping immediate stimuli to immediate responses'.
questions.answer: Assembling on-the-fly complex, abstract models of the current situation, of ourselves and of other people; using them to anticipate possible futures and plan long-term; quickly adapting to unexpected situations; and picking up new skills after little practice.
questions.explanation: These are listed in the paragraph beginning 'Humans are capable of far more...'. They describe what an extreme generalizer does that a stimulus-response mapping (insect or deep net) does not.

questions.question: Why is a Python dict an example of a system with no generalization at all?
questions.answer: It returns a value only for keys stored exactly in advance; any other query fails, so it can't handle anything it wasn't told about precisely.
questions.explanation: The author uses the dict and hardcoded if-then-else Q&A programs as examples of very rigid automatons with no generalization. Deep nets do slightly better because they handle small deviations.

questions.question: Think of a model you've trained in this book (e.g. the dogs-vs-cats convnet). Describe one input that would count as a 'brand-new problem' for it and predict how it would behave.
questions.answer: Open answer. For example, a pencil sketch of a cat or a photo of a fox: the model would still output 'cat' or 'dog' with possibly high confidence, because it has no way to recognize that the input is outside what it was trained on.
questions.explanation: Applying the brand-new-problem test to your own models makes the automaton argument concrete and leads into the local-generalization discussion on p.598.

questions.question: What does the author mean by 'known unknowns', and give the page's example?
questions.answer: Factors of variation that were anticipated during model development and are extensively featured in the training data, such as different camera angles or lighting conditions for pet pictures.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in e03. Deep nets can only generalize across such anticipated, well-sampled variation.

questions.question: According to the page, why is basic data augmentation so helpful for deep net generalization?
options: It reduces the number of parameters the model needs
Deep nets generalize via interpolation on a manifold, so every factor of variation must be captured by the learned manifold, and augmentation supplies such variation
It lets the model build abstract physical models of the input
It replaces the need for a validation set
questions.answer: Deep nets generalize via interpolation on a manifold, so every factor of variation must be captured by the learned manifold, and augmentation supplies such variation
questions.explanation: The text links the two directly: 'any factor of variation in their input space needs to be captured by the manifold they learn. That's why basic data augmentation is so helpful.' Augmentation does not change parameter count, does not produce abstract models (the thing deep nets lack), and does not replace validation.

questions.question: In Figure 19.6, both rows start from the same three known situations. Why is that design choice essential to the figure's message?
questions.answer: Because it holds the information fixed. The only difference is how large an operational area each system obtains from that information, so the figure illustrates intelligence as efficiency (information conversion ratio), not as amount of experience or skill.
questions.explanation: The labels 'lower/higher information conversion ratio' and the identical dot configurations show this; p.604 formalizes it as an efficiency ratio.

questions.question: Contrast how a deep net and a human would solve the rocket-landing problem, and explain where each one's generalization comes from.
questions.answer: The deep net needs tens of thousands to millions of trials (a dense sampling of input space) and generalizes by interpolating between them. The human uses abstraction to build a physical model (rocket science) and derives an exact solution in one or a few trials. The model's validity across all configurations is what provides generalization.
questions.explanation: This is the page's e05 example. It contrasts coverage-based generalization (interpolation) with model-based generalization (abstraction).

questions.question: In the city-navigation example, what happens when the deep net is dropped into a new city?
options: It transfers its knowledge perfectly
It would have to relearn most of what it knows
It refuses to act
It becomes an intelligent agent
questions.answer: It would have to relearn most of what it knows
questions.explanation: The text says: 'Dropped into a new city, the net would have to relearn most of what it knows.' The learned mapping is tied to the specifics of the training city rather than an abstraction like 'cars are dangerous'. The other options contradict the page.

questions.question: Which earlier model does the author use as an example of useful local generalization, and what condition limits it?
questions.answer: The dogs-vs-cats model from chapter 8. It classifies unseen cat or dog pictures only as long as they are close enough to what it was trained on.
questions.explanation: Stated at the start of e03.

questions.question: Pick a model you have deployed or trained. List two factors of variation you covered (known unknowns) and one plausible unknown unknown that could break it.
questions.answer: Open answer. Example for a pet classifier: known unknowns are lighting and pose (covered by data and augmentation); an unknown unknown is pets in costumes or a thermal camera image.
questions.explanation: Applying the known/unknown-unknown distinction to real systems is how this page's theory becomes practical robustness thinking.

questions.question: State the author's definition of intelligence from this page.
questions.answer: Intelligence is the ability to efficiently use the information at your disposal to produce successful behavior in the face of an uncertain, ever-changing future.
questions.explanation: Quoted from the paragraph beginning 'That's the nature of intelligence'.

questions.question: Under what condition does the author say the automaton stage of brain evolution would already be optimal?
options: When the organism has a very large brain
When the set of situations the organism faces is mostly static and known in advance
When the organism lives in a social group
When DNA mutations are rare
questions.answer: When the set of situations the organism faces is mostly static and known in advance
questions.explanation: The page states that in that case evolution could find correct behaviors by trial and error and hardcode them, and 'this first stage of brain evolution ... would already be optimal'. Brain size, sociality and mutation rate are not mentioned as the condition.

questions.question: Why can't evolution hardcode the behaviors you execute during an ordinary day?
questions.answer: Because each day is unlike any day you or your ancestors have experienced. The specific situations are novel and unpredictable, so there is no fixed behavior sequence that selection could have discovered and stored in DNA in advance. It must be generated on the fly.
questions.explanation: This is the core of the 19.2.3 argument: evolution works slowly across generations on recurring situations, while daily life presents unique, unforeseen ones.

questions.question: According to the page, what is the key to extreme generalization that the author associates with Descartes's 'understanding'?
options: Memorizing as many past situations as possible
Hardcoding more behavioral programs in DNA
Mining past experience to develop modular, reusable abstractions that can be quickly repurposed
Increasing the number of neurons
questions.answer: Mining past experience to develop modular, reusable abstractions that can be quickly repurposed
questions.explanation: The page defines 'understanding' as 'the power to mine your past experience to develop modular, reusable abstractions that can be quickly repurposed to handle novel situations'. Memorization and hardcoding describe automatons; neuron count is not the author's criterion.

questions.question: Why does the author mention apes, octopuses and ravens, and what does this support?
questions.answer: They are highly intelligent animals in very distant evolutionary branches. This supports the claim that the shift to optimizing for adaptability occurred multiple times, so intelligence is a recurring answer to complex, dynamic ecosystems rather than a one-off.
questions.explanation: The text: 'This shift likely occurred multiple times ... resulting in highly intelligent animals in very distant evolutionary branches—apes, octopuses, ravens, and more.'

questions.question: What is the 'spectrum of generalization', and where did biological evolution start and (for hominins) end up on it?
questions.answer: An ordering of systems by how broadly they generalize. Evolution started with automaton-like brains capable only of local generalization and, in the last few million years, certain hominin species trended toward extreme generalization.
questions.explanation: From the 19.2.4 paragraph, which the author calls 'a crude caricature'; it continues on p.600.

questions.question: Draw the parallel: what in deep learning plays the role of 'evolution hardcoding behavior', and what would correspond to 'brains optimizing for adaptability itself'?
questions.answer: Open answer. Offline training that produces fixed weights corresponds to evolution hardcoding behavior. Systems trained or designed to adapt quickly at inference time to new tasks (test-time adaptation, meta-learning, program synthesis) correspond to optimizing for adaptability.
questions.explanation: Connects this page's biology to the chapter's later prescriptions (pp.604–606).

questions.question: Define broad generalization as the author does, and give one of his examples.
questions.answer: The ability to deal with unknown unknowns within a single broad domain of tasks, including situations the system was not trained for and that its creators could not have anticipated. Examples: a self-driving car that safely handles any situation, or a domestic robot passing the Woz test (making coffee in a random kitchen).
questions.explanation: Defined in the paragraph beginning 'Today, we may be on the cusp...'.

questions.question: Where does the author place 2010s deep learning on the spectrum of generalization?
options: Pure automaton, like ELIZA
Local generalization, expanded by larger datasets and more expressive models
Broad generalization
Extreme generalization
questions.answer: Local generalization, expanded by larger datasets and more expressive models
questions.explanation: The text: 'In the 2010s, deep learning further expanded the local generalization power of these systems.' ELIZA-style automatons are earlier, broad generalization is the next step we 'may be on the cusp of', and extreme generalization is human cognition.

questions.question: Why does the author call the 'intelligence' label in 'artificial intelligence' a category error, and what alternative naming does he propose?
questions.answer: Because the deep learning paradigm has remained limited to cognitive automation, so calling it intelligence attributes a property it does not have. He proposes calling the field 'artificial cognition', with 'cognitive automation' and 'artificial intelligence' as two nearly independent subfields, the latter a greenfield.
questions.explanation: From the paragraph beginning 'However, the deep learning paradigm...'.

questions.question: Explain each part of the sentence 'they map space X to space Y via a smooth geometric transform learned from a dense sampling of X-to-Y data points, and any disruption within spaces X or Y invalidates this mapping.'
questions.answer: A model is a function from inputs X to outputs Y. It is a smooth, differentiable geometric transformation, a composition of layers. It is fitted to many example pairs that must cover the input space densely. If the input distribution changes or the meaning of outputs changes, the fitted function no longer applies and can't adapt without new data.
questions.explanation: Each phrase corresponds to a concept from earlier chapters (layers as geometric transforms, dense sampling from chapter 5) and to local generalization (p.598).

questions.question: According to the page, how is visible progress toward broad generalization currently being made?
options: By scaling deep learning models alone
By combining deep learning with painstakingly handcrafted abstract models of the world
By returning to ELIZA-style rule systems
By evolutionary algorithms only
questions.answer: By combining deep learning with painstakingly handcrafted abstract models of the world
questions.explanation: Stated directly. Scaling alone is what section 19.2 ('Scale isn't all you need') argues against. Pure rule systems are automatons, and evolutionary algorithms are not mentioned here.

questions.question: What were ELIZA and SHRDLU, and why does the author call them pure automatons?
questions.answer: ELIZA was a 1960s chat program; SHRDLU was a 1970 system that manipulated simple objects from natural-language commands. They are pure automatons because they followed hand-written rules and could not generalize beyond what was explicitly programmed.
questions.explanation: The page names both as early pure automatons; footnote 2 cites Winograd's work behind SHRDLU.

questions.question: Classify a recent AI product you know as cognitive automation or (toward) artificial intelligence in the author's sense, and justify it using the X-to-Y mapping criterion.
questions.answer: Open answer. A good answer asks whether the system only maps inputs similar to its training data to outputs (cognitive automation) or whether it can adapt with little or no data to situations nobody anticipated.
questions.explanation: Practices applying the page's distinction to real claims of AI progress.

questions.question: State the kaleidoscope hypothesis.
questions.answer: Our experience of the world seems to feature incredible complexity and endless novelty, but everything is similar to everything else. The number of unique atoms of meaning needed to describe the universe is relatively small, and everything is a recombination of these atoms: a few seeds, endless variation.
questions.explanation: From the paragraph beginning 'I call this the kaleidoscope hypothesis'.

questions.question: According to the page, what would happen if the future you faced were truly novel, sharing no common ground with anything you'd seen?
options: A sufficiently intelligent agent would still adapt
You'd be unable to react to it, no matter how intelligent you are
Deep learning would handle it better than humans
You would fall back on innate priors and succeed
questions.answer: You'd be unable to react to it, no matter how intelligent you are
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph. Intelligence needs shared structure to transfer from. Innate priors are also past information and wouldn't help if nothing were shared, and deep learning is even more dependent on similarity to training data.

questions.question: Why does the author add that 'these analogies aren't just in our minds'? What would be lost if analogies were only mental?
questions.answer: Because the hypothesis needs the world itself to be structured by repeated patterns (isomorphisms) for analogy-based generalization to work reliably. If analogies were only mental projections, like seeing animals in clouds, they would not reliably predict anything about new situations.
questions.explanation: The author gives physical isomorphisms (electromagnetism/gravity, animal anatomy, silica/ice crystals) to ground the hypothesis in reality, not only psychology.

questions.question: In the kaleidoscope metaphor, what do the glass beads represent?
options: Individual training examples
The unique atoms of meaning from which everything is recombined
The mirrors of perception
Random noise in the world
questions.answer: The unique atoms of meaning from which everything is recombined
questions.explanation: The text compares the small number of atoms of meaning to 'a few glass beads' that produce endless patterns. Training examples correspond to observed patterns, not beads. The mirrors are the recombination mechanism. The patterns are structured, not noise.

questions.question: Give the two historical examples the author uses for describing new technology by analogy.
questions.answer: A 17th-century person seeing a jet plane might describe it as a large, loud metal bird that doesn't flap its wings; a car is a 'horseless carriage'.
questions.explanation: Both are in the paragraph beginning 'Intelligence works because nothing is ever truly without precedent.'

questions.question: How does the kaleidoscope hypothesis motivate the strategy 'acquire abstractions, then recombine them' for building intelligence?
questions.answer: If everything is a recombination of a small set of atoms, the most efficient way to handle novelty is to extract those atoms from experience (abstraction acquisition) and recombine them on the fly to model each new situation, rather than trying to cover every surface pattern with data.
questions.explanation: This is exactly how p.602 continues: intelligence mines experience for the 'core beads of the kaleidoscope' (abstractions) and recombines them.

questions.question: Pick something you recently learned that was new to you. Which existing concepts (atoms) did you recombine to understand it?
questions.answer: Open answer. For example, understanding attention in Transformers as 'a soft dictionary lookup': query/key/value from dictionaries, weighted averaging from statistics, and similarity from dot products.
questions.explanation: Noticing your own analogies makes the hypothesis concrete and shows the recombination step that p.602 says deep learning lacks.

questions.question: According to the book, which part of intelligence is classic deep learning completely missing?
options: Abstraction acquisition
On-the-fly recombination
Memorization of training data
Gradient-based optimization
questions.answer: On-the-fly recombination
questions.explanation: The book says these models 'do a decent job at acquiring abstractions at training time' but 'have zero ability to recombine what they know at test time.' Acquisition is present but inefficient; memorization and gradient-based optimization are things deep learning clearly does.

questions.question: State the shortcut rule in your own words.
questions.answer: If you optimize for a single success metric, you'll reach it, but everything in the system the metric doesn't measure is free to get worse, because you take every available shortcut toward the goal.
questions.explanation: The book: 'you will achieve your goal, but at the expense of everything in the system that wasn't covered by your success metric.'

questions.question: Why does the book's definition of intelligence imply that enumerating every chess move to find the best one is unintelligent, even though it finds the best move?
questions.answer: Because the book measures intelligence by efficiency, not by the result. Brute-force enumeration reaches the right answer only by spending enormous computation, which is the opposite of efficiently selecting and recombining abstractions.
questions.explanation: 'The emphasis on efficiency is crucial.' The chess example illustrates inefficient recombination, as the practice-hours example illustrates inefficient acquisition.

questions.question: Why did Netflix never use the system that won its $1 million prize?
questions.answer: It was too complex and compute intensive; the winners had optimized for prediction accuracy alone.
questions.explanation: The sentence continues on p.603: accuracy was improved at the expense of inference cost, maintainability and explainability.

questions.question: What does the book mean when it says classic models behave like 'a static abstract database'?
options: They store raw training examples verbatim and look them up
They can retrieve learned patterns but cannot recombine them into new models at test time
They cannot learn any abstractions from data
They require a database backend to run inference
questions.answer: They can retrieve learned patterns but cannot recombine them into new models at test time
questions.explanation: 'Static' refers to fixed behavior after training and 'abstract' to stored abstractions, not raw examples; 'limited purely to retrieval' is the point. The book explicitly credits them with acquiring abstractions, and the database is a metaphor.

questions.question: How does 'Biological intelligence was the answer to a question asked by nature' support the argument of 19.3.3?
questions.answer: The capabilities of a system reflect the problem it was shaped to solve. Nature's 'question' required adapting to unpredictable environments, which produced general intelligence; AI research has asked task-specific questions, so it gets task-specific answers. To get general intelligence, ask a question that requires it.
questions.explanation: The paragraph concludes that 'the capabilities of AI systems reflect the objectives they were designed and optimized for,' which sets up the shortcut rule and the new target of p.604.

questions.question: Think of a metric you've optimized (validation accuracy, latency, a leaderboard score). What did it fail to capture, and did that property get worse?
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer names a specific uncovered property (model size, inference cost, robustness to distribution shift, fairness) and how optimization traded it away.
questions.explanation: Applying the shortcut rule to your own work is the best test of whether you've understood it.

questions.question: Why did Allen Newell propose chess as a grand goal for AI?
questions.answer: Because chess in humans seemed to require perception, reasoning and analysis, memory and study, so he expected a chess-playing machine to need those abilities too, giving AI a path toward a theory of cognition.
questions.explanation: The page says Newell was concerned that his field wasn't progressing toward a theory of cognition.

questions.question: According to the book, what lets engineers 'buy' more skill on a fixed task without increasing generalization power?
options: Using larger learning rates
Adding more data or more hardcoded knowledge
Switching to a more general architecture
Testing on tasks the creators couldn't anticipate
questions.answer: Adding more data or more hardcoded knowledge
questions.explanation: The page states this directly. Learning rates are an unrelated optimization detail; a more general architecture would address generalization, not bypass it; and testing on unanticipated tasks is the remedy the book proposes on p.604, not a way to buy skill.

questions.question: Why can a nearest-neighbor algorithm reach superhuman skill at a video game, and what exposes its lack of intelligence?
questions.answer: With near-infinite training data, any new game state has a nearly identical stored state whose action can be copied. A small change to the rules makes all stored data inapplicable; a human adapts instantly while the system must be retrained.
questions.explanation: Its skill comes from task-specific information, not generalization power.

questions.question: Explain in your own words: 'by fixing the task, you remove the need for intelligence.'
questions.answer: Intelligence is the ability to handle uncertainty and novelty. A fixed task can be described precisely in advance (by data or rules), so it contains no novelty to handle, and it can be solved without intelligence. Since that's easier, it's what will happen.
questions.explanation: This is the summary argument at the end of the page.

questions.question: Which statement matches the book's view of the relationship between skills and general intelligence?
options: General intelligence emerges once enough task-specific skills are collected
General intelligence can acquire skills, but a collection of skills doesn't lead to general intelligence
Skills and general intelligence are the same thing measured differently
Skills are irrelevant to intelligence
questions.answer: General intelligence can acquire skills, but a collection of skills doesn't lead to general intelligence
questions.explanation: The page's last sentence. The first option is exactly what it denies; the third contradicts the skill/intelligence distinction; the fourth goes too far, since intelligence is defined as the ability to acquire skills.

questions.question: Name three properties that the Netflix Prize winners sacrificed for prediction accuracy.
questions.answer: Inference cost, maintainability and explainability.
questions.explanation: Listed at the top of the page.

questions.question: Pick a recent AI milestone you've heard about. Was it on a fixed task? Could its skill have been bought with data or compute? What test would show whether it reflects generalization power?
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer identifies whether the task was fixed and proposes a test with novel tasks the system's creators couldn't anticipate.
questions.explanation: This practices the book's way of evaluating claims about AI.

questions.question: In Figure 19.8, under what condition does task-specific skill reliably indicate generalization power?
options: When information is unlimited
When task-relevant information (priors + experience) is fixed
When the task is fixed and well known in advance
When the system has the most parameters
questions.answer: When task-relevant information (priors + experience) is fixed
questions.explanation: At the dashed 'fixed priors + experience' line, higher curves give higher skill. With unlimited information (option 1), any curve reaches high skill. A fixed, known task (option 3) is exactly what allows skill to be bought. Parameter count isn't on the figure.

questions.question: What are the two quantities in the book's efficiency ratio?
questions.answer: The amount of relevant information available (past experience or innate prior knowledge) and the future operating area (the set of novel situations where the agent will produce appropriate behavior).
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph of 19.3.4.

questions.question: Why must the test tasks be ones that 'the creators of the system could not have anticipated'?
questions.answer: If creators can anticipate the tasks, they can build knowledge of them into the system through data, architecture or rules. That adds task-relevant information that isn't counted, raising skill without raising generalization power, which is a form of cheating.
questions.explanation: The book says this condition is needed 'to avoid cheating.'

questions.question: Agent A solves 50 of 100 novel tasks after seeing 20 examples per task family; agent B solves 50 after seeing 2,000. Under the efficiency-ratio view, which is more intelligent, and by roughly what factor?
questions.answer: Agent A, by roughly 100 times (same operating area, 1/100 of the information).
questions.explanation: The ratio is novel situations handled per unit of information. Equal numerators and a 100x smaller denominator give a 100x larger ratio. This illustrates the book's verbal definition; the book gives no numeric formula.

questions.question: Why does the goal 'create a model that solves task X' lead to a model that does X, period?
questions.answer: Because of the shortcut rule: optimizing for skill on X will take every shortcut toward X, including adding data and task-specific knowledge, without producing generalization beyond X.
questions.explanation: The page links this goal explicitly to the shortcut rule of p.602.

questions.question: What does the green dashed vertical line in Figure 19.8 represent?
options: The maximum achievable skill
A fixed amount of priors + experience
The point where a system starts to overfit
Human-level performance
questions.answer: A fixed amount of priors + experience
questions.explanation: It's labeled 'Fixed priors + experience.' The figure doesn't mark a maximum skill, overfitting, or human level.

questions.question: Can you explain, using Figure 19.8, why a large benchmark gain from training on more data doesn't necessarily mean a system became more intelligent?
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer says that more data moves the system right along its own curve rather than onto a higher curve.
questions.explanation: This is the key reading of the figure.

questions.question: Describe the structure of an ARC-AGI task and how you're scored on it.
questions.answer: Three or four demonstration examples (input grid -> output grid) explain the task; then you get a new input grid and have three tries to produce the exact output grid.
questions.explanation: From the first paragraph of the page and Figure 19.9.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the two features the book says make ARC-AGI unique compared to IQ tests?
options: It only tests on tasks you've never seen before
It controls for prior knowledge using Core Knowledge priors
It excludes acquired knowledge like English sentences
It is designed to be difficult for humans
questions.answer: It is designed to be difficult for humans
questions.explanation: The two features are testing only on unseen tasks and controlling for prior knowledge (of which excluding acquired knowledge is part). ARC is meant to be approachable by humans, who score very high (p.606).

questions.question: Why does ARC-AGI exclude acquired knowledge such as English sentences?
questions.answer: Because prior knowledge counts as information in the efficiency ratio of intelligence. To compare test takers fairly, they must start from the same priors, here the innate Core Knowledge. Acquired knowledge would let a system score by what it already knows rather than by generalizing.
questions.explanation: Links p.605's design choice to p.604's definition.

questions.question: Why does the book say ARC-AGI is a game you can't practice for 'at least in theory'?
questions.answer: Because each test task has its own unique logic to understand on the fly, so memorized strategies shouldn't transfer. 'In theory' acknowledges that tasks may still share abstractions or patterns, so perfect novelty can't be guaranteed.
questions.explanation: The book's qualification suggests novelty is a design goal, not an absolute property.

questions.question: What was the purpose of founding the ARC Prize Foundation in 2024?
options: To sell ARC-AGI as a commercial IQ test
To accelerate progress toward AI capable of fluid abstraction and reasoning by incentivizing researchers
To replace ImageNet as the main computer-vision benchmark
To certify AI systems as AGI
questions.answer: To accelerate progress toward AI capable of fluid abstraction and reasoning by incentivizing researchers
questions.explanation: The page says so directly. The foundation is a nonprofit (not commercial), ARC isn't a vision benchmark in the ImageNet sense, and nothing on the page mentions certification.

questions.question: Look at Figure 19.9 and try to produce the output for the test input before reading any explanation. What concepts did you use?
questions.answer: Open-ended; typical concepts are objects, direction, continuing a line, and reflecting off a wall.
questions.explanation: Noticing that you used only innate-like concepts shows what Core Knowledge priors mean.

questions.question: Why did most benchmarks saturate quickly in the LLM era while ARC-AGI did not?
options: ARC-AGI tasks are too large to fit in an LLM's context window
Most benchmarks can be hacked via memorization, and ARC-AGI is designed to resist it
ARC-AGI is scored only by human judges
LLMs were never evaluated on ARC-AGI
questions.answer: Most benchmarks can be hacked via memorization, and ARC-AGI is designed to resist it
questions.explanation: Stated directly on the page. Context size and human judging aren't mentioned, and LLMs were evaluated (0% to ~10%).

questions.question: Define test-time adaptation and name its two forms described in the book.
questions.answer: Methods where the AI system performs active reasoning or learning during the test itself, using the specific problem's information. Forms: test-time training (gradient descent on the task's examples) and search methods (over reasoning steps or programs).
questions.explanation: From the definition paragraph and the bullet list.

questions.question: What is the difference between chain-of-thought synthesis and program synthesis as search spaces, and why might the second be easier to check?
questions.answer: Chain-of-thought synthesis searches over reasoning in natural language; program synthesis searches over symbolic programs. Programs are verifiable: you can run a candidate on the demonstration inputs and check its outputs exactly.
questions.explanation: The book calls the program space 'symbolic, verifiable'; the point about checking is an elaboration.

questions.question: o3 scored 76% at about $200 per task and 88% at over $20,000 per task. By what factor (at least) did cost increase, and how many points did the score gain?
questions.answer: At least 100x more cost per task for 12 percentage points.
questions.explanation: $20,000 / $200 = 100, and 88 - 76 = 12. Strongly diminishing returns, which feeds the efficiency critique on p.607.

questions.question: Why does the book treat a 50,000x scale-up with only ~10% on ARC-AGI as a 'big warning sign'?
questions.answer: If massively increasing a resource yields almost no progress, that resource isn't the bottleneck. Something qualitatively different, on-the-fly recombination, is missing.
questions.explanation: The page concludes that ARC-AGI showed on-the-fly recombination capabilities are necessary for reasoning.

questions.question: What did every top entry in ARC Prize 2024 have in common?
options: They were the largest available pretrained models
They used some form of test-time adaptation
They hardcoded rules for each test task
They were trained on the private evaluation set
questions.answer: They used some form of test-time adaptation
questions.explanation: The book: 'Every single top entry in ARC Prize 2024 used them.' Leading solutions 'did not emerge from simply scaling existing deep learning architectures'; the other two options would be impossible or cheating given unseen, private tasks.

questions.question: Can you explain to someone why test-time adaptation addresses the missing half of intelligence described on p.602?
questions.answer: Open-ended; a good answer links static, retrieval-only models to the absence of recombination, and TTA's per-problem learning or search to recombination at test time.
questions.explanation: Connects this page's mechanism to the chapter's theory.

questions.question: What are the two reasons the book gives for saying o3 wasn't as intelligent as a human?
questions.answer: (1) Its performance came at tremendous cost, tens of thousands of dollars of compute per puzzle, and intelligence is about efficiency. (2) It was still stumped by many tasks humans found very easy.
questions.explanation: Introduced with 'First' and 'Second' on the page.

questions.question: Why does the book say ARC-AGI-1 was 'essentially a binary test of fluid intelligence'?
options: Each task has a yes/no answer
Systems either scored near zero (no fluid intelligence) or very high (some genuine fluid intelligence), with little in between
Only two types of tasks were included
Scores were rounded to 0% or 100%
questions.answer: Systems either scored near zero (no fluid intelligence) or very high (some genuine fluid intelligence), with little in between
questions.explanation: That's the book's explanation. ARC answers are output grids, not yes/no; the page says nothing about task types or rounding.

questions.question: Why could ARC-AGI be solved 'in principle' without any intelligence?
questions.answer: Because each task's demonstration pairs let you verify a candidate program. With enough compute, you could enumerate every possible program and test each one until one reproduces all demonstrations, then apply it to the test input.
questions.explanation: The book: 'walking down the tree of every possible solution program and testing each one until you find one that works on the demonstration pairs.'

questions.question: A brute-force solver uses 30 primitives and searches all programs up to 4 steps long. Roughly how many programs of exactly 4 steps must it consider, and how does this change if tasks need 6 steps?
questions.answer: 30^4 = 810,000 programs of 4 steps; 30^6 = 729,000,000 programs of 6 steps, about 900 times more.
questions.explanation: Illustrative calculation (not in the book) of why enumeration cost explodes with program length, which is why harder, longer-chain tasks in ARC-AGI-2 are 'less brute-forcible.'

questions.question: Which two properties did the book say a new ARC-AGI version needed?
options: Larger grids and more colors
Less brute-forcible, and better at differentiating levels of fluid reasoning up to human level
Natural-language instructions and multiple-choice answers
Public test sets and unlimited attempts
questions.answer: Less brute-forcible, and better at differentiating levels of fluid reasoning up to human level
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of the second paragraph. Larger grids aren't mentioned; natural language would add acquired knowledge, which ARC avoids (p.605); public tests and unlimited attempts would make shortcuts easier.

questions.question: How does this page's critique of o3 echo the chess example on p.602?
questions.answer: On p.602, needing to enumerate every possible chess move to find the best one was given as a sign of low intelligence. o3's expensive search on ARC is the same pattern: success through large-scale exploration rather than efficient recombination of abstractions.
questions.explanation: Both rely on the efficiency criterion of intelligence.

questions.question: Try the task in Figure 19.10 yourself. How long did it take, and how many hypotheses did you consider? Compare that with the cost of o3's failed attempt.
questions.answer: Open-ended; most people find the rule (using the color key) within a few minutes after a few hypotheses.
questions.explanation: Experiencing the gap firsthand illustrates the efficiency argument.

questions.question: What did ARC-AGI-2 change relative to ARC-AGI-1?
options: The input/output format of the tasks
The task content, toward deeper reasoning and resistance to exhaustive search
It replaced grids with natural-language questions
It removed the demonstration pairs
questions.answer: The task content, toward deeper reasoning and resistance to exhaustive search
questions.explanation: The book says ARC-AGI-2 'kept the exact same format' but 'significantly improved the task content'. The format, grids and demonstration pairs are all unchanged, so the other options are wrong.

questions.question: Why did the ARC Prize Foundation want ARC-AGI-2 to be resistant to exhaustive search?
questions.answer: So that computational efficiency becomes critical: success should require intelligent, efficient strategies rather than exploring billions of possibilities with huge compute.
questions.explanation: The book treats intelligence as efficiency (p.607). A brute-forcible benchmark would reward compute budget, not intelligence.

questions.question: How did base LLMs perform on ARC-AGI-2 according to the book?
options: About human level
Low double digits
Effectively 0%
Around 50%
questions.answer: Effectively 0%
questions.explanation: The book says base LLM performance was 'effectively back at 0%', consistent with its claim that they lack fluid intelligence. 'Low double digits' describes o3 under reasonable compute budgets, not base LLMs.

questions.question: The book qualifies o3's ARC-AGI-2 score with 'when constrained to reasonable computational budgets.' Why is this qualification central to the argument?
questions.answer: Because the claim is about efficiency. With unlimited compute, search can eventually solve many tasks, but intelligence is about reaching results with minimal resources, so performance under a budget is what measures it.
questions.explanation: Compare p.607: o3's ARC-AGI-1 success cost tens of thousands of dollars per puzzle and 'felt more like cracking a code with a supercomputer'.

questions.question: What is the average time human test takers needed per ARC-AGI-2 task, and what does it show?
questions.answer: About 5 minutes. It shows the tasks need deliberate thinking but are still well within ordinary human ability.
questions.explanation: This contrasts with ARC-AGI-1, whose tasks humans solved almost instantly.

questions.question: Section 19.4 is titled 'The missing ingredients: Search and symbols.' Based on this page and the previous ones, why are these ingredients 'missing' from current systems?
questions.answer: Base deep learning stores abstractions as continuous parametric curves and recalls them statically. It does not search a discrete space of symbolic programs at test time. TTA adds some search, but it is inefficient and still fails on ARC-AGI-2 under budget.
questions.explanation: The page concludes that something beyond current TTA is needed, and the next pages (p.609-613) develop program-centric abstraction and program synthesis.

questions.question: Look at Figure 19.11. Can you state the rule of the left-hand task in one sentence? Try to do the same for the right-hand task and notice how much longer it takes.
questions.answer: Left: each red bar becomes the diagonal of a light-blue diamond sized by the bar's length. Right: needs several observations about colors, frames and the swatch row.
questions.explanation: Trying both yourself shows the difference between 'instant' ARC-AGI-1 tasks and 'deliberate' ARC-AGI-2 tasks that the paragraph describes.

questions.question: Which comparison method gives rise to value-centric analogies?
options: Exact structural match
Similarity comparison via a continuous distance function
Subgraph isomorphism
Symbolic theorem proving
questions.answer: Similarity comparison via a continuous distance function
questions.explanation: The book links similarity comparison to value-centric analogies. Exact structural match and subgraph isomorphism belong to program-centric analogy, and theorem proving is not one of the two comparison methods.

questions.question: Why are prototypes called 'abstract' in the beetle example?
questions.answer: They don't look like any specific beetle you've seen, yet they encode properties common to all members of their cluster.
questions.explanation: Merging instances (e.g., averaging) produces a representative that is not any one instance.

questions.question: Why does comparing a new beetle to a handful of prototypes, rather than to every beetle seen, matter?
questions.answer: It compresses experience into a few reusable abstractions, making prediction cheap and letting knowledge transfer to new instances via their category.
questions.explanation: The book says you 'won't need to compare it to every single beetle' and can use the nearest prototype, the category, to make useful predictions.

questions.question: According to the book, what kind of generalization does value-centric analogy enable in deep learning?
options: Extreme generalization
Local generalization
No generalization
Symbolic generalization
questions.answer: Local generalization
questions.explanation: The book states 'Value-centric analogy is the kind of analogy-making that enables deep learning models to perform local generalization'. Extreme generalization needs both poles (p.612).

questions.question: Explain the statement 'what kind of abstractions you manipulate determines how, and how well, you can recombine them' using deep learning as the example.
