questions.answer: Deep learning stores abstractions as continuous parametric curves, so it can only recombine them continuously (interpolation, blending), not by exact discrete composition the way program pieces combine. That limits the novel recombinations it can make.
questions.explanation: This motivates looking for a second, program-like kind of abstraction.

questions.question: What chapter 10 artifact does the book cite as an example of visual prototypes?
questions.answer: The ConvNet features (filter visualizations) you visualized in chapter 10.
questions.explanation: Filter visualizations show patterns that a filter responds to: abstract visual prototypes learned from data.

questions.question: Can you describe both steps of K-means and match each to a phrase in the beetle paragraph?
questions.answer: Assignment step = 'clustering more similar instances together'; update step = 'merging them into a set of prototypes'. Prediction = 'find the closest prototype'.
questions.explanation: If you can make this mapping, you understand why the book calls the beetle story 'pretty much' K-means.

questions.question: Which description fits program-centric analogy?
options: Immediate, approximate, intuitive
Slower, exact, deliberate
Fast, exact, unconscious
Slow, approximate, data-hungry
questions.answer: Slower, exact, deliberate
questions.explanation: The book calls it 'slower, exact, deliberate'. 'Immediate, approximate, intuitive' describes value-centric analogy; the other two combinations are not in the book.

questions.question: What formal problem does the book say you solve when looking for shared structure across programs?
questions.answer: Subgraph isomorphism: finding subgraphs of the programs' operator graphs that are exactly shared.
questions.explanation: Programs can be represented as graphs of operators, and shared program subsets are exactly matching subgraphs.

questions.question: Why does the book contrast comparing functions with comparing two human faces?
questions.answer: Faces are compared by how similar they look, through an implicit continuous distance (value-centric). Functions are related by whether parts have exactly the same structure (program-centric). The contrast shows the two kinds of comparison.
questions.explanation: The book says 'You're not trying to compare your classes and functions by how similar they look ... Rather, you're interested in whether there are parts of them that have exactly the same structure.'

questions.question: Subconsciously categorizing movie characters into 'types' is an example of what?
options: Program-centric abstraction
Value-centric abstraction
Subgraph isomorphism
Formal logic
questions.answer: Value-centric abstraction
questions.explanation: The book gives this as an example of value-centric abstraction: automatic categorization by similarity, done without thinking.

questions.question: Give a non-programming example of a program-centric analogy and explain why it qualifies.
questions.answer: E.g., realizing that a new scheduling problem has the same constraint structure as one solved before. It qualifies because the relation is about a discrete network of relationships matching exactly, not about surface similarity.
questions.explanation: The book says any time you think about objects connected by a discrete network of relationships, you're using program-centric analogies.

questions.question: Recall the last time you refactored duplicated code. Can you name the shared subgraph you extracted and what became parameters?
questions.answer: Personal answer: the shared structure became the function body; whatever differed (inputs, names) became parameters.
questions.explanation: This is the book's software-engineering example of program-centric analogy, applied to your own experience.

questions.question: According to Table 19.1, how does program-centric abstraction produce abstractions?
options: By averaging instances into prototypes
By isolating isomorphic substructures across instances
By gradient descent on a parametric function
By clustering with a distance function
questions.answer: By isolating isomorphic substructures across instances
questions.explanation: That's the table's program-centric entry. Averaging into prototypes and clustering by distance are value-centric; gradient descent is the deep learning engine (Table 19.2), not a row of Table 19.1.

questions.question: In Figure 19.13's code, list three things that differ between the two instances and are therefore not part of compute_mean.
questions.answer: The list's source (obj.as_list() vs. get_data()), the variable names (ls_sum/ls_entries/avg vs. total/num_elems/mean), and the use of the result (print vs. update_mean).
questions.explanation: The shared abstraction keeps only the exactly matching structure; the list becomes a parameter and the result is returned.

questions.question: Why can program-centric abstraction operate on as few as two instances while value-centric abstraction needs a lot of experience?
questions.answer: An exact structural match between two instances already pins down the shared structure precisely. An average-based prototype is noisy and becomes reliable only with many samples.
questions.explanation: Exactness removes the need for statistical averaging (see the 'deeper' note).

questions.question: Which pair of properties does Table 19.1 attribute to value-centric abstraction?
options: Discrete, grounded in topology
Continuous, grounded in geometry
Slow, exact, rigorous
Underlies reasoning and planning
questions.answer: Continuous, grounded in geometry
questions.explanation: The other three options are program-centric entries of the table.

questions.question: How does the mathematician example support the claim that 'everything we think is a combination of both types of abstraction'?
questions.answer: Theorem proving looks like pure discrete reasoning, but the mathematician starts with a fuzzy, intuitive vision of the direction, and that intuition (value-centric) guides the discrete reasoning steps (program-centric).
questions.explanation: The book uses it as the counterpart of object recognition, which looks like pure perception but involves implicit reasoning.

questions.question: What is the bug risk shared by both instances and compute_mean, and how would you fix it?
questions.answer: If no element is non-None, num_elems is 0 and the division raises ZeroDivisionError. Guard with a check (e.g., return None or raise a clear error when num_elems == 0).
questions.explanation: Not discussed in the book. A practical observation about the printed code.

questions.question: Without looking, can you reconstruct all six rows of Table 19.1?
questions.answer: Distance/exact match; continuous-geometry/discrete-topology; averaging into prototypes/isolating isomorphic substructures; perception-intuition/reasoning-planning; immediate-fuzzy-approximative/slow-exact-rigorous; lots of experience/as few as two instances.
questions.explanation: These contrasts are used throughout the rest of chapter 19 and in the conclusions.

questions.question: According to the book, what happens if a deep learning model trained to sort lists of five numbers must now sort lists of 10?
options: It generalizes automatically
It needs a small fine-tuning step with a few examples
It must be completely retrained on even more data
It sorts correctly but more slowly
questions.answer: It must be completely retrained on even more data
questions.explanation: The book says 'you'll need to completely retrain the model— on even more data'. The other options describe generalization the model doesn't have; only a sorting program handles any length.

questions.question: What rule of thumb does the book give for when to use deep learning?
questions.answer: When you have lots of data and the problem is one where the manifold hypothesis applies.
questions.explanation: Stated after the MNIST example: fitting a parametric model is simpler and more robust in that situation.

questions.question: Explain the book's two examples of the poles emulating each other, and why that doesn't make the distinction useless.
questions.answer: A polynomial (continuous) can pass through any discrete points, so continuous models can embed discrete programs. Linear algebra on computers runs continuous math via discrete programs on bits. But emulation is inefficient: each problem type is much better served by its natural pole (sorting vs. MNIST).
questions.explanation: The book calls the poles 'more of a spectrum' and still says 'there are clearly types of problems that are better suited to one or the other'.

questions.question: Roughly what test accuracy does the book suggest a hand-written, non-ML Python MNIST classifier might reach after thousands of lines?
questions.explanation: The book says 'After thousands of lines of code, you might achieve 90% test accuracy.'

questions.question: Why does the book call program-centric abstraction 'arguably the most important half'?
questions.answer: It enables experience-efficient, exact generalization from very few examples (e.g., a sorting program working on any list after a couple of examples), which is what fluid intelligence and novel tasks like ARC-AGI require and what scaling deep learning failed to provide.
questions.explanation: Combine p.611's 'experience efficient' row with the sorting example and the ARC-AGI results (p.606-608).

questions.question: How many coefficients does a polynomial need to pass exactly through n points with distinct x values, and what does this say about generalization?
questions.answer: n coefficients (degree n-1). Fitting the points exactly says nothing about values elsewhere, so a perfect fit to samples of a discrete rule does not mean the rule has been learned.
questions.explanation: This formalizes the book's caveat that you 'may fit a polynomial function through any set of discrete points, as long as you have enough coefficients.' (Formal statement not in the book.)

questions.question: What two reductions does the book consider unlikely?
questions.answer: Reducing reasoning problems to manifold interpolation, and reducing perception problems to discrete reasoning.
questions.explanation: Hence the call for a unified framework that incorporates both types of abstraction generation.

questions.question: Pick a problem from your own work. Is it closer to sorting or to MNIST? Which pole, or what combination, would you use?
questions.answer: Personal answer; use the data-abundance and manifold-hypothesis test, and check whether an exact rule exists.
questions.explanation: This applies the page's practical guidance.

questions.question: According to Table 19.2, what is the 'engine' of program synthesis?
options: Gradient descent
Backpropagation through time
Discrete search (such as genetic search)
K-means clustering
questions.answer: Discrete search (such as genetic search)
questions.explanation: Gradient descent is the ML engine. Backpropagation through time and K-means are ML techniques, not program synthesis engines.

questions.question: What is the key difference between how machine learning and program synthesis obtain a mapping from inputs to outputs?
questions.answer: ML learns parameter values in a hardcoded program (a neural network). Program synthesis generates source code through a discrete search process.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the second paragraph of 19.4.4.

questions.question: Why does the book distinguish pre-2024 discrete-reasoning systems from program synthesis, even though both do discrete reasoning?
questions.answer: Pre-2024 systems' reasoning was written by human programmers (search, graph manipulation, formal logic). Program synthesis has the system generate the programs itself, i.e., acquire program-centric abstractions, which is what intelligence requires.
questions.explanation: The book's definition of intelligence centers on acquiring and recombining abstractions, not executing human-written ones.

questions.question: In Figure 19.14, what does the program specification consist of?
options: A natural-language description of sorting
Two input/output pairs of lists
A formal logic proof
A neural network architecture
questions.answer: Two input/output pairs of lists

questions.question: Why is program synthesis data efficient while machine learning needs a lot of data?
questions.answer: A synthesized program is an exact, rule-like hypothesis tested for exact agreement with the examples, so a couple of examples can pin it down and it generalizes to all inputs. ML fits a continuous approximation that needs dense sampling of the input space to interpolate reliably.
questions.explanation: Mirrors Table 19.1's 'experience efficient' row and the sorting example on p.612.

questions.question: With a vocabulary of 11 building blocks (as in Figure 19.14), how many token sequences of length 10 exist, and what does this imply for the search?
questions.answer: 11^10, about 2.6 x 10^10 sequences. Blind search grows exponentially with program length, so practical program synthesis needs a smarter, guided search.
questions.explanation: This combinatorial explosion is why the book later proposes using deep learning to guide program search (p.616). (Calculation not in the book.)

questions.question: What does the book call program synthesis in the last paragraph of the page?
questions.answer: 'The missing piece of the puzzle': how we'll add program-centric abstraction capabilities to AI systems.
questions.explanation: It completes the argument of 19.4: deep learning provides value-centric abstraction, and program synthesis provides the program-centric half.

questions.question: Run the toy synthesizer in the vocabulary code entry. Can you add a spec example that makes it return a different program, or none?
questions.answer: E.g., an example whose output isn't a sorted version of the input forces a different composition or no solution within max_len.
questions.explanation: Experimenting shows how the specification constrains the search and why ambiguity matters.

questions.question: According to the page, in DeepMind's AlphaGo where does learning from data happen?
options: In the Monte Carlo Tree Search procedure
Only in specialized submodules: the value networks and policy networks
Throughout the system, which is trained end to end
In a 3D world model updated by perception modules
questions.answer: Only in specialized submodules: the value networks and policy networks
questions.explanation: The book says most of AlphaGo's intelligence is hand-designed (e.g., MCTS) and learning happens only in value and policy networks. MCTS is hand-coded, AlphaGo isn't end-to-end, and the 3D world model belongs to the Waymo example.

questions.question: What are the two major ways the authors expect deep learning and program synthesis to be combined?
questions.answer: (1) Systems integrating deep learning modules with discrete algorithmic modules; (2) using deep learning to make the program search process more efficient.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets at the top of the page; the first is developed on pp.614-615, the second on pp.615-616.

questions.question: Why does the book say RNNs have 'slightly fewer limitations' than feedforward networks, yet remain 'extremely limited'?
questions.answer: They add one programming primitive, a hardcoded for loop over time, so they are geometric transformations applied repeatedly rather than once. But each step is still a differentiable geometric transformation and information passes between steps only as continuous state vectors.
questions.explanation: The loop gives iteration and reuse of the same function across steps; the continuous, differentiable nature of each step and of memory keeps them from representing exact discrete programs.

questions.question: In the Waymo example, which component is hand-engineered and which is learned, and why is this split sensible?
questions.answer: The 3D world model and its assumptions are hand-engineered; the perception modules that update it from sensor data are learned (deep learning, powered by Keras). Perception is a pattern-recognition problem suited to deep learning, while maintaining an explicit, structured model of the world is suited to engineered code.
questions.explanation: This mirrors the book's broader claim (p.612) that perception fits deep learning and structured reasoning fits discrete programs.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed on the page as a programming primitive a future network might manipulate?
options: while statements
hash tables
disk storage for long-term memory
convolutional kernels
questions.answer: convolutional kernels
questions.explanation: The page lists if branches, while statements, variable creation, disk storage, sorting operators, and data structures such as lists, graphs and hash tables. Convolution kernels are ordinary continuous, learned network components, not discrete programming primitives.

questions.question: What is the key difference between today's hybrid systems and the future systems the authors describe?
questions.answer: Today the discrete algorithmic elements are hardcoded by human engineers; in future systems they may be fully learned with no human involvement.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the paragraph about AlphaGo and self-driving vehicles.

questions.question: Pick an AI system you know (a chess engine, a recommender, a voice assistant). Can you identify which parts are learned continuous models and which are hand-coded discrete logic?
questions.answer: Answers vary; e.g., a chess engine may combine a learned evaluation network with hand-coded alpha-beta or tree search.
questions.explanation: Practicing this decomposition helps you see the page's claim that strong systems are usually hybrids.

questions.question: Why will primitive-rich learned programs need to be generated by a combination of discrete program search and gradient descent?
options: Because gradient descent is too slow for large models
Because they are not differentiable end to end, although specific modules remain differentiable
Because program search can only optimize continuous parameters
Because they contain no learned parameters
questions.answer: Because they are not differentiable end to end, although specific modules remain differentiable
questions.explanation: The page says exactly this. Speed of gradient descent isn't the issue; program search optimizes discrete structure, not continuous parameters; and the geometric modules do contain learned parameters.

questions.question: What does figure 19.15 depict?
questions.answer: A modular task-level program, learned on the fly to solve a specific task, made of geometric subroutines (pattern recognition, intuition) and algorithmic subroutines (reasoning, search, memory), receiving data and feedback from a task and sending actions back.
questions.explanation: Read from the figure and its caption.

questions.question: Why does the book call AlphaGo and RNNs 'prehistoric ancestors' of hybrid algorithmic-geometric models rather than examples of them?
questions.answer: AlphaGo blends algorithmic and geometric components, but its algorithmic part (MCTS) is hand-coded rather than learned; an RNN is learned but has only one hardcoded algorithmic primitive (the for loop). The envisioned systems learn a rich blend with little human involvement.
questions.explanation: Combines p.614 (AlphaGo's hand-designed search; RNN's hardcoded loop) with p.615's requirement that the whole system be learned.

questions.question: A synthesizer enumerates flat programs of length 8 built from 20 primitives. How many candidates are there? If a learned model restricts each step to the top 4 primitives, how many remain?
questions.answer: 20^8 = 2.56 × 10^10 candidates; 4^8 = 65,536 with guidance.
questions.explanation: Count is V^L. Restricting the branching factor from 20 to 4 shrinks the space by a factor of 5^8 ≈ 390,000. (This simplified model ignores tree structure, which makes the unguided count even larger.)

questions.question: Name the two factors the page identifies that cause program search to explode combinatorially.
questions.answer: Increasing complexity of the program specification (requiring longer programs) and an expanding vocabulary of primitives.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the paragraph on combinatorial explosion: more steps multiply options, more primitives widen each step.

questions.question: What human behavior does the page say program synthesis should imitate to become efficient?
options: Writing every possible program and testing them in parallel
Considering only a handful of approaches informed by understanding of the problem and past experience
Copying code from the internet without understanding it
Using gradient descent to tune each line of code
questions.answer: Considering only a handful of approaches informed by understanding of the problem and past experience
questions.explanation: The page explicitly contrasts exhaustive search with a programmer who only has a few approaches in mind. The other options are either the inefficient baseline or not mentioned.

questions.question: Think about the last nontrivial script you wrote. How many overall approaches did you seriously consider, and what told you which ones were worth considering?
questions.answer: Answers vary; typically 1-3 approaches, chosen from familiarity with similar problems.
questions.explanation: Reflecting on your own heuristic pruning makes concrete the 'learned intuition' the next page proposes to give to program synthesizers.

questions.question: What property of program space makes deep learning potentially useful for guiding program search, according to the page?
options: Every program is a differentiable function
The space of all useful programs may look a lot like a continuous manifold
Programs can be interpolated directly by averaging their source code
Program space is small enough to enumerate
questions.answer: The space of all useful programs may look a lot like a continuous manifold
questions.explanation: The book says each program is discrete and non-interpolative, but the space of useful programs may resemble a continuous manifold. Programs aren't differentiable, can't be averaged, and program space explodes combinatorially (p.615).

questions.question: What training data would the deep learning model that guides program search learn from?
questions.answer: Millions of successful program-generation episodes: specifications together with the search paths that led to correct programs.
questions.explanation: The page says the model would be trained on millions of successful program-generation episodes to learn intuition about the path through program space.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the book offers for reusing knowledge across tasks rather than training each model from scratch.
questions.answer: Many datasets don't contain enough information to develop a new complex model from scratch, and training from scratch is inefficient because current tasks overlap heavily with previously encountered ones.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the first paragraph of 19.4.6, with the analogy of not relearning English for each book.

questions.question: What 'key ingredient' does the book say LLMs are missing?
options: Enough training data
Recombination of functions on the fly into new programs
The ability to retrieve memorized functions
Attention mechanisms
questions.answer: Recombination of functions on the fly into new programs
questions.explanation: The page says LLMs are very good at fetching and reapplying memorized functions but can't recombine them on the fly. Retrieval is what they do well; data and attention aren't the issue identified.

questions.question: An LLM performs one elementary step correctly with probability 0.9. Assuming independent errors, what is the probability it gets a 10-step composed computation right? What does this suggest about building on brittle functions?
questions.answer: 0.9^10 ≈ 0.35. Small per-step error rates compound across composition, so brittle functions make poor building blocks; exact components (p = 1) remain correct at any depth.
questions.explanation: This illustrates (beyond the book) the book's remark that you wouldn't build a codebase on brittle functions like LLMs' large-integer addition.

questions.question: Why are functions and classes from human programming languages a better basis for recombination than patterns memorized by LLMs?
questions.answer: They are robust (exact), abstract and modular, with clean interfaces designed for reuse in new contexts, so they compose reliably; LLM patterns are approximate, context-dependent and not designed to be combined.
questions.explanation: The page says these components are 'evolved specifically for modular reuse in a new context—unlike the patterns that LLMs memorize'.

questions.question: Can you explain in your own words the difference between retrieving a skill and composing skills, using an example from your own learning?
questions.answer: Answers vary; e.g., knowing a recipe for pasta (retrieval) vs. inventing a new dish by combining known techniques (composition).
questions.explanation: Being able to articulate this distinction shows you understand the book's diagnosis of LLMs.

questions.question: In figure 19.16, what does the perpetual meta-learner send to the global library?
options: Design choices
Actions
Reusable subroutines
Raw training data
questions.answer: Reusable subroutines
questions.explanation: The arrow from meta-learner to library is labeled 'Push reusable subroutines'. Design choices go to the task-level program; actions go from the program to the task; raw data isn't stored in the library.

questions.question: What two kinds of subroutines can the global library contain, and what is each like?
questions.answer: Geometric subroutines (deep learning modules with pretrained representations) and algorithmic subroutines (closer to the libraries contemporary software engineers manipulate).
questions.explanation: Stated at the end of the software-development paragraph and shown in the figure.

questions.question: Why does the book say these AIs would be 'constantly self-improving'?
questions.answer: Because reusable components are built from the cumulative experience of all AI instances and remain accessible to all forever, so any problem only needs to be solved once; the library keeps growing.
questions.explanation: Self-improvement here is the monotonic growth of a shared library, not a claim about runaway intelligence.

questions.question: Map the HTTP-library example onto the meta-learning system: what corresponds to writing a library, publishing it, and importing it?
questions.answer: Writing a library ↔ abstracting a recurring subroutine from several tasks; publishing ↔ pushing it to the global library; importing ↔ the meta-learner fetching relevant subroutines for a new task.
questions.explanation: The book draws the analogy explicitly in the second paragraph.

questions.question: When does the meta-learning system create a new abstract subroutine, according to the page?
options: Whenever it starts a new task
When it finds itself developing similar subroutines for several different tasks
When a human engineer requests it
Only after training finishes on all tasks
questions.answer: When it finds itself developing similar subroutines for several different tasks
questions.explanation: The page says exactly this; abstraction is triggered by recurrence across tasks, not by each new task or by humans, and the process is continual.

questions.question: What is the first point of the authors' long-term vision?
questions.answer: Models will be more like programs, with capabilities far beyond the continuous geometric transformations of input data we use today, closer to the abstract mental models humans maintain.
questions.explanation: The first bullet of 19.4.7, completed on p.618.

questions.question: Without looking, can you sketch figure 19.16 and label every arrow?
questions.answer: Library ↔ meta-learner (fetch, push); meta-learner → task-level program (design choices); program → meta-learner (data and feedback); task → program (data and feedback); program → task (actions).
questions.explanation: Reproducing the figure from memory checks that you understand the architecture rather than just recognizing it.

questions.question: In the long-term vision, what kind of process searches over combinations of subroutines to grow new models?
options: End-to-end gradient descent
Discrete search (program synthesis) heavily guided by deep-learning intuition
Random sampling without guidance
Manual design by human engineers
questions.answer: Discrete search (program synthesis) heavily guided by deep-learning intuition
questions.explanation: Stated in the fourth bullet. Gradient descent alone can't search discrete structures, unguided search explodes combinatorially (p.615), and the vision explicitly removes manual design.

questions.question: According to the page, why can humans quickly learn a complex new video game?
questions.answer: Because experience with many previous games yields models that are abstract and program-like rather than a basic mapping between stimuli and action.
questions.explanation: This is the book's analogy for extreme generalization in the fifth bullet.

questions.question: Which two kinds of abstraction does the blend of algorithmic and geometric modules achieve, and which module provides which?
questions.answer: Program-centric abstraction (algorithmic modules: formal reasoning, search, abstraction) and value-centric abstraction (geometric modules: informal intuition, pattern recognition).
questions.explanation: From the second bullet, using the vocabulary of 19.4.1.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the system can assemble a working model for a new task with very little data.
questions.answer: Rich program-like primitives that generalize well, and extensive experience with similar tasks.
questions.explanation: Both are named in the fifth bullet.

questions.question: What is the authors' stance on a 'singularitarian robot apocalypse'?
options: It is an inevitable consequence of AGI
It is a serious risk the book analyzes in detail
It is pure fantasy stemming from misunderstandings of intelligence and technology
It will happen within 10-20 years
questions.answer: It is pure fantasy stemming from misunderstandings of intelligence and technology
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says this and adds that a fuller critique doesn't belong in the book, so it's neither analyzed in detail nor predicted.

questions.question: How do frequent problem-solving patterns end up in the global library?
